I have had two findings overturned in thirty years and I remember both of them better than anything I got right. In each case the fact was correct and the sentence was too strong. Once you write a person was negligent, you are no longer describing an event, you are making a legal claim, and somebody will come and test it. So I write it would appear that, and people outside the profession tell me that is weak. It is not weak. It is accurate about how much I know. If the evidence gets stronger later, I can promote the sentence. If I have already written the strong version, I have nowhere to go except backwards, in public. And there is a second reason nobody mentions. A hedged finding is easier for the company to accept, and a finding nobody accepts changes nothing at all.

There is one question I ask about every recommendation I read, and it takes about four seconds. Would this have prevented the occurrence in front of us? Almost always yes, because people write recommendations backwards from the accident. Then I ask the second question. Would it have prevented the next one, which will not look like this one at all? And that is where most reports fall apart. If the answer is no, you have found a contributing factor and you have called it a root cause, and the corrective action you are about to agree will make everybody feel better and change nothing. I would rather send a report back three times than approve a recommendation that only works on an accident that has already happened.
